body:
I believe I've found the offending piece of code:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/71a9948157dc2d5cc71fcb456c9d96656678757d/modules/gdscript/gdscript_analyzer.cpp#L5235

I'll attempt to get a local build going and make a pull request adding the special case for `not`.

This inference hole is also present in all the operators that always return `bool`. This includes comparisons (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`), binary logical operators (`and` and `or`), and the `in` operator. Additionally, the bitwise operators (`<<`, `>>`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`) all always return `int`. Note the `is` operator is already always inferred as `bool` even if its argument is `Variant`. Please correct me if I'm wrong on any of these or missing some.

I'm not sure I would be comfortable allowing the bitwise operators to be inferred since, if other types such as `bool` or `Vector2i` were later supported, that would have to be a breaking change. But for the rest of the operators, does it sound reasonable to have them unconditionally inferred?

> This inference hole is also present in all the operators that always return `bool`. This includes comparisons (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`), binary logical operators (`and` and `or`), and the `in` operator. Additionally, the bitwise operators (`<<`, `>>`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`) all always return `int`.

Note that for some types some operators are not defined. In case of `not` operator it really looks like a bug, operators `and`, `or`, `not` should be handled on GDScript side, not core (operands should be booleanized). But for comparison operators it is not true, as it may cause a runtime error.

> But for the rest of the operators, does it sound reasonable to have them unconditionally inferred?

No. As I explained above, this should only work for operators defined for all types, provided that they are guaranteed not to have type errors at runtime. Currently, this only applies to `and` and `or`, as they are implemented in GDScript, not in core. It would make sense to do the same for `not` (note that changing the analyzer might not be enough, and might require changes to the compiler). Potentially, this could be applied to `==` and `!=`, but they are not type safe in Godot, i.e. the `bool` result is not guaranteed (an error may occur).

> But for comparison operators it is not true, as it may cause a runtime error.

Type inference on an expression makes no guarantee that evaluating the expression won't cause a type error. (If only!) All it really guarantees is that *if* the expression returns a value, it will be of that inferred type. The `as` operator is the clearest example of this. `x as bool` will always be inferred as a `bool` even though it may error at runtime.

Additionally, whether or not the type can be inferred in these cases within a piece of code is essentially unrelated to its type safety. Consider the following code:

```gdscript
var x: Variant = ...
if x == 1: ...
```

Naturally this will give a runtime type error if the value of `x` isn't comparable to an integer. Now let's suppose that this condition is extracted into a variable, due to some outer context of the code.

```gdscript
var x: Variant = ...
var condition := x == 1
if condition: ...
```

Under current Godot this will give a type inference error. We would have to replace the line with one of the following:

```gdscript
var condition: bool = x == 1
var condition := true if x == 1 else false
```

Importantly, these changes do not improve the type safety of the code! In fact, they could only hurt, in the (probably very rare) case that you give the wrong explicit annotation or mix up `true` and `false`.

I am always in favor of more type safety in GDScript. I am also of the opinion that improvements to type inference (only when sound, of course) can only serve to improve type safety.

> note that changing the analyzer might not be enough, and might require changes to the compiler

From my vague understanding of the analyzer I think it every needed change would fit in there. We just need to allow more GDScript code to be inferred.

I'm not sure how "Up for grabs" works but I'd gladly take up fixing this. I've already got `not` working and I have a good idea of where and how I would change the rest of the code. I would like to contribute to Godot and this seems like a good first issue for me.

This is a bit of a debatable issue. There are no exceptions in Godot/GDScript, but we could indeed treat it the way you described, if we consider `==` and `!=` operators as defined for all types, overriding this behavior on the GDScript side and not relying on the core, like in the case of `and` and `or`. That is, if we assert in advance that `a == b` can only evaluate to `bool` (or an error). But personally I'm still not sure if this is a good idea. `and`, `or`, `not` are special operators and rather part of the language, while the evaluation of other operators is delegated to the Godot core.

The case with operators like `<` and `<=` is a bit more complicated than with `==` and `!=`. For some types the inequality operators are not defined (if I remember correctly) and their necessity is not as obvious as in the case of `==` and `!=`. Using a non-existent operator is conceptually no different from accessing a potentially non-existent property or calling a potentially non-existent method. Just as `var x := a.position` causes a compile-time error, `var x := a + b` and `var x := a < b` should cause a compile-time error (if `a` and/or `b` are `Variant`s). Because `Variant` is a union type, not all of its options have specific properties, methods, and operators. So the result type is not known statically.

Finally, your assumption only takes into account existing types. We cannot know for sure whether Godot will add built-in types and/or the ability to declare custom operator overloads in the future that violate this assumption.

> The `as` operator is the clearest example of this. `x as bool` will always be inferred as a `bool` even though it may error at runtime.

The `as` and `is` "operators" are also special. They are not part of core (not listed in `Variant::Operator`) and are evaluated in GDScript. Furthermore, they even have separate node types in the AST (not `BinaryOpNode`), since their right operand is a type, and we don't have full first-class types.

> From my vague understanding of the analyzer I think it every needed change would fit in there. We just need to allow more GDScript code to be inferred.

I haven't checked this, but if there are cases where `not x` can cause a type error at runtime, then we should write an opcode to booleanize `x` value in the compiler/codegen before the negation evaluation, if the specific type of `x` is unknown statically (just like we do for `and` and `or` operands). If core's `OperatorEvaluator` works without type errors for all types, then only changes to the analyzer (plus tests) will be enough.

Every single Variant type has both a defined `not` operation, and a defined booleanize function. There should be no possibility for the function given by OP to cause an error at runtime, or evaluate to anything that isn't a bool.

This is the logic behind how we know that `var x := a and y` will work. It follows from that that therefore `var x := not (a and b)` should also work. Why then not `var x := not a`?

This seems to be a problem with the analyzer. If this specific error check is disabled, the code compiles and runs without error, no matter what the value of the Variant is.

(It should be noted as well that `var c := a and not b` does **also** work. The problem is exclusive to unary `not` in the analyzer.)

> `and`, `or`, `not` are special operators and rather part of the language, while the evaluation of other operators is delegated to the Godot core.

From the perspective of the user I don't see how this distinction matters, especially since this issue isn't about changing evaluation at all (on either the GDScript or core side), only type inference.

> Just as var `x := a.position` causes a compile-time error, `var x := a + b` and `var x := a < b` should cause a compile-time error (if a and/or b are Variants). Because Variant is a union type, not all of its options have specific properties, methods, and operators. So the result type is not known statically.

There's a difference that only applies to the first two examples: the type of `x` depends on the types of `a` and `b`. In the third example `x` will always be `bool`. This is known statically, short of some Godot bug, because there is simply no case in the language where it will evaluate to something else. By leaving `a` or `b` untyped, the user has opted in to dynamic typing and runtime type errors for any usage of `a` or `b`, *but no farther*. Once evaluation proceeds into statically known types, runtime type errors once again become impossible (or at least mostly impossible?) until the next usage of an untyped value, e.g. using `x` will never cause a runtime type error on its own.

> We cannot know for sure whether Godot will add built-in types and/or the ability to declare custom operator overloads in the future that violate this assumption.

Forgive me if I'm under some misconception with GDScript. I have to imagine that if the language allowed operator overloading, it would be allowed through GDScript classes that inherit from `Object`, yes? However, `Object == Object` is already inferred as `bool`. Allowing non-`bool` types for `==` or `!=` is already a breaking change. (As an aside, I also think allowing that would be a bad idea; not enforcing this in C++ is something I recall the committee regretting.)

> If core's OperatorEvaluator works without type errors for all types, then only changes to the analyzer (plus tests) will be enough.

Any observable changes to evaluation would be out of scope for this issue, IMO. I just want to change type inference to better reflect the reality of the existing, well-defined evaluation rules.

Thank you for this discussion, by the way!!

This is a rather controversial issue, so I don't want to continue the debate any further, but I'll try to explain my view once again. What I wanted to emphasize is that the behavior is determined by the "specification". There is no single correct behavior, and different options are possible, as long as there is some logic to it. It is inevitable that several people will disagree, each with their own idea of the most intuitive behavior, and a different set of assumptions about the behavior of the engine and the language, which do not always correspond to reality.

If we really fix in the "standard" the assumption that `a == b` can only return `bool` (or an error), then the type inference _might_ work as you described, otherwise it won't. It would be incorrect, just like for other operators, properties, methods, etc. with subexpressions of unknown types. The same goes for the `not` operator, although there is an additional small argument that this operator belongs to the category of logical operators, for which this rule is already fulfilled (logical operators and comparison operators are different categories, although this is also debatable).

A separate non-obvious question is whether possible runtime errors should be considered an obstacle to type autoinference or not. On the one hand, if the result type is fixed in the "standard", then this makes sense. On the other hand, this hinders type safety, and potential errors can be considered as missing operator overloads. In this case, it is incorrect to consider the operator defined for the entire `Variant` union type if it is not defined for all of its options.

Type autoinference is a strict typing feature. Unlike assigning or passing an argument with an unknown or wider type, an unknown result type results in a compile-time error, not in unsafe lines or `UNSAFE_*` warnings (there is a separate `INFERENCE_ON_VARIANT` warning for hard `Variant`, which is treated as an error by default).

Finally, note that `"a" == 1` causes a compile-time error `Invalid operands "String" and "int" for "==" operator.`. The same thing will happen at runtime if you replace literals with `Variant` variables. In my opinion, it is strange to mark `var x := a == b` as completely safe if we cannot guarantee that `a == b` will evaluate successfully and, moreover, produce a compile-time error when replacing variables with literals. This is less logical than the current behavior (not speaking about the behavior of the operator itself, only the type inference).

In the current Godot implementation, operators and constructors of built-in types support overloads, even though native and custom methods do not. Overload resolution happens both statically and dynamically. Accordingly, `int.operator ==(right: float)` exists, but `String.operator ==(right: int)` does not. You can even see this explicitly in the documentation. `Variant.operator ==(right: Variant)` also does not exist, and is defined as a union of the types in `Variant`, so it is unsafe, since it does not exist for all its options.

I see. It was not my intention to create discontent or be combative, and I apologize if that is how I came across. I would really like to discuss this further with you or another member, but I don't want to push the issue if doing so is unwelcome, and I also recognize it is rather niche. Regardless, this is evidently a nontrivial matter, and deserving of its own PR or perhaps even feature proposal.

I'll file a PR just changing the inference of `and`, `or`, and `not`, and see how that goes.
